source.title: More Data Can Hurt for Linear Regression: Sample-wise Double Descent

record.tranche_reason: Tests sample-wise double descent with an isotropic Gaussian linear-regression model and a minimum-norm ridgeless estimator, rather than the deep-network settings of the cited original study.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own sample-size sweep and theoretical bias, variance, and risk results. Statements about sample-wise nonmonotonicity in deep networks and model-wise double descent from cited work are not this study's results and are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own sample-size sweep (d = 1000, σ = 0.1, 50 trials) and derives risk expressions for min-norm linear regression. These show test risk rising as n approaches d, which is a new-setting test of V3. Its bias–variance decomposition attributes the peak to the noise-driven variance term, which bears on V6's mechanism part. It is not one of the original sources.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. In well-specified isotropic linear regression, the min-norm (gradient-descent) estimator's test risk can increase with more samples near n = d. The cause is that bias decreases while variance increases, the noise term diverging from poor conditioning of X. The authors frame the note as expository, with analysis techniques not novel.
record.recipe_differences: Analyzes a fixed-dimensional isotropic Gaussian linear-regression model with a minimum-norm ridgeless estimator and varies sample count; it does not reproduce the deep-network experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Risk changes across the sample-to-dimension ratio and peaks near n = d. Noise and regularization are not varied experimentally.

fits_no_version.finding: Claim 3 gives the exact change in Tr[(XXᵀ)⁻¹] from adding one sample, explaining poor conditioning near n = d.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The sample-wise peak arises from ill-conditioning of the data matrix near n = d.

record.problems: The empirical demonstration is presented in a figure without tabulated risk values or a reported error bar, confidence interval, or standard deviation. The experiments use one stated dimension and noise level; the theoretical expressions are asymptotic approximations.

untested.parts: Deep networks and other model classes; only isotropic Gaussian well-specified linear regression with the min-norm estimator.
Noise-level sweeps, multiple/triple peaks, and disappearance of the peak under optimally tuned regularization are not tested.
No capacity sweep; d is fixed and n varies.

missing.what: Statement that the theoretical bias, variance and risk from Claims 1–2 agree with experiment at finite d = 1000 (Figure 1b vs 1a).

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T2 to T3: this is a new setting (linear regression) rather than a different method on deep networks. The study is an expository note relying on Hastie et al. (2019) for the underparameterized expressions (Claim 2). No error bars are reported.

versions.untested_parts: The empirical setting is isotropic Gaussian linear regression, not deep networks or other model classes.
No capacity sweep across model classes; model dimension is fixed while sample count varies.
No unified effective-complexity measure is proposed or tested across size, epochs, and samples.
The paper explains the peak through a noise-related variance term in its fixed noisy setting, but does not sweep noise levels, test multiple peaks, or test optimally tuned regularization.
No alternative effective parameter count or re-expression of the curve as an ordinary U-shape is tested.

rows.subject: minimum-norm ridgeless regression estimator (β̂ = X†y)
rows.operation_detail: Varies the number of training samples and plots expected test MSE.

conditions.value: mean over 50 trials; individual points show a single trial

rows.measure: Test MSE versus number of training samples
rows.note: The text describes the plotted test risk as non-monotonic, peaking at n = d; it states that risk first decreases, then increases, then decreases again.
rows.check: Figure-only row with no numeric values; the peak at n = d and the fall-rise-fall shape are stated in text. The row is otherwise correct.

rows.subject: minimum-norm ridgeless regression estimator (β̂ = X†y)
rows.operation_detail: Gives theoretical expected excess-risk expressions as sample count varies relative to dimension.
rows.value: For γ < 1: (1 − γ)²||β||² + σ²γ/(1 − γ). For γ > 1: σ²/(γ − 1). These are stated as asymptotic approximations.
rows.note: The expressions predict risk rising toward the interpolation point from below and decreasing in the underparameterized regime.
rows.check: The overparameterized excess-risk value is misquoted. Eq. 7 gives (1 − γ)||β||² + σ²γ/(1 − γ): the bias (1−γ)² plus the variance term γ(1−γ) sum to (1−γ). The record has (1 − γ)²||β||². Eq. 8 is the same expression in n and d.

rows.subject: minimum-norm ridgeless regression estimator (β̂ = X†y)
rows.operation_detail: Decomposes expected excess risk into bias and variance and gives an approximate variance expression.
rows.measure: Variance contribution to expected excess risk
rows.note: The text attributes the peak to the noise-related trace term, which diverges as γ approaches 1.
rows.check: The row is acceptable. Note that the noise attribution is analytic (the σ²·Tr[(XXᵀ)⁻¹] term diverges near n = d), not an experimental noise sweep.

rows.subject: minimum-norm ridgeless regression estimator (β̂ = X†y)
rows.operation_detail: Derives the bias as a function of sample count and states its monotonicity.
rows.measure: Bias contribution to expected excess risk
rows.value: Bₙ = (1 − γ)²||β||² in the asymptotic approximation; the text states Bₙ₊₁ ≤ Bₙ.
rows.note: The authors contrast nonincreasing bias with the increasing noise-related variance contribution.
rows.check: This bias row is a mechanism component: bias is nonincreasing, so it cannot cause the peak. It is linked to V6 only as the contrast that isolates variance as the driver. The row is acceptable.

relationships.condition: Well-specified isotropic Gaussian linear regression, min-norm ridgeless estimator, d = 1000, σ = 0.1
relationships.reason: Test MSE rises with more samples and peaks at n = d in experiment (r1). The theory gives risk diverging as γ → 1 from below (r2).
relationships.display_finding: Experimental test MSE peaked at n = d, while theoretical risk diverged as γ approached 1 from below.

relationships.condition: Same noisy linear-regression setting, unregularized estimator
relationships.reason: The peak comes from the noise-driven variance trace term diverging near n = d (r3), while bias is nonincreasing (r4). This supports the variance/noise-driven peak.
relationships.display_finding: The noise-driven variance trace diverged near n = d while bias remained nonincreasing.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
